name: gather timber
note: 3000 g is one armful; the rate is declared [D], because no source states what a game gather costs

name: riven haft
note: riving, not sawing: splitting along the grain is what the stone age can do, and it is why a haft is a blank rather than a cut board

name: knap a core
note: the 800/200 split is declared [D]: real knapping loses more, but a usable edge is what the process is for and the flakes are the loss

name: gather plant fibre
note: 100 g is a bundle of brush; the rate is declared

name: twist cord
note: the first process in `bound & composite`, and the reason that tier exists: binding is what makes a composite tool possible before metal is

name: assemble the hatchet
note: the chain's end, and Q7's own example: a hatchet fashioned from natural materials, which is the tool that multiplies work before anything is mined

name: forage
note: 2000 g is a person's day of eating, picked in half an hour of game time: the rate is declared [D], and the real figure it should sit near (a person eats 1-2 kg of food a day) is the only sourced half of it

name: fire brick
note: 900-1000 °C is what fired brick is actually fired at [V], and heat_kind is `material` because it is the clay body that has to reach it, not the flame — the distinction SOURCES.md found is worth about 600 °C. The gas is declared as a volume because a gas is one: 60000 mL at 1.3 g/L is exactly 78 g, the clay's loss on ignition [D] — 7.8 % of it leaves as water and carbon dioxide

name: char timber
note: a quarter of the wood's mass comes out as charcoal, the low end of the real range (20-35 % depending on the kiln) — declared, not sourced, because the charcoal-yield row is [NS]. 400 °C is where wood pyrolyses [V, range]. The rest leaves as 1700 L of flue gas (2210 g at 1.3 g/L) and 40 g of ash, and the three outputs are the 3000 g that went in, to the gram

name: burn charcoal
note: the warming fire: a kilo of charcoal a day, 2.5 % of it left as ash and the rest up the chimney as gas. heat_kind is `flame` here and `material` in the two rows above — what a person warms their hands on is the flame, and what a brick needs is the body of clay itself
